passage: Sit down, beta. You asked how I managed when my father got old, so I'll tell you the truth. I'm Abhinav. Years ago he needed a hospital trip every week and money for his tablets, and he wanted someone in the house in the evenings. I loved him and, God forgive me, I felt trapped. I didn't say a word for months. Then one Sunday I sat down with my sibling Irfan and said, "I can't carry this alone." We made a rota: Irfan took the hospital visits, I took the evenings, and we split the costs. I also told my father, "Baba, I can do Tuesdays, not every day." Saying I needed help wasn't disloyal. The house got kinder afterwards, and so did I.

qa.q: How often did Abhinav's father need a hospital trip?
What two feelings did Abhinav have about looking after the father?
qa.a: Love and feeling trapped, and Abhinav kept the second feeling silent for months.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that eased the situation?
qa.a: Abhinav told Irfan, "I can't carry this alone," made a rota that split the visits, evenings and costs, and told the father plainly what days Abhinav could do.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when Abhinav finally spoke up?
qa.a: Irfan may have been surprised at how much Abhinav had been carrying, but agreed and took the hospital visits, so probably was willing to help once asked clearly.

grounding: Shows a parent leaning on the protagonist for money, medical trips or company, the protagonist feeling love and being trapped, sharing the load with a sibling and setting realistic limits.

passage:
Nazia, when you asked me on the show what caring for my mother is like, I said "fine". I'm Manoj, her son, and it wasn't fine. Let me say it properly.

Amma has had kidney trouble for two years. Every Tuesday and Friday I take her to dialysis. I sit in that hospital corridor four hours, working on my laptop, then drive her home. I love her. And some Tuesdays, stuck in traffic, I felt like the walls were closing in.

My sister Radhika lives an hour away. I never asked her for anything, because it felt like admitting I was failing Amma.

In January I finally called. "Radhika, I can't do both days. Can you take Fridays?" There was silence, then, "Why didn't you say so a year ago?" Now she does Fridays and I do Tuesdays.

Asking for help wasn't betraying Amma. It's what's letting me keep going.

qa.q: On which days does Manoj take his mother to dialysis?
qa.a: He takes her every Tuesday and Friday.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling on some Tuesdays in traffic?
qa.a: Manoj felt trapped, like the walls were closing in, even though he loved his mother.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that made the care more manageable?
qa.a: He asked his sister for one specific thing, taking Fridays, instead of carrying it all alone out of a sense of duty.

qa.q: How did Radhika seem to feel when Manoj finally asked?
qa.a: Radhika seemed surprised and a little hurt that he hadn't asked a year earlier, and willing to help.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young man whose parent leans on him for medical trips, feeling love and being trapped, who shares the load with a sibling.

passage:
Monday. Papa called Vandana at 5:10, 5:40 and 6:15. "When are you coming? The house is too quiet." Since Mummy died, he wanted her there every evening. Vandana cancelled her pottery class for the fourth week and sat with him through the news, loving him and feeling the walls press in.

Thursday. On the bus she called her sister in Pune. "Reena, I need you to do something specific. Video-call Papa every evening at seven. Every single one." Reena hesitated. "I didn't know he was calling you so much." "He is. And I'm not managing." Reena agreed, and said she'd come for two weekends a month.

Three weeks later. On Tuesday evening Vandana's hands were grey with clay. At seven, Papa was laughing at something Reena said on the tablet, and Sharma uncle from next door had come for carrom. Vandana still visited four evenings a week, but now she wanted to.

qa.q: How many times did Papa call Vandana on Monday evening?
qa.a: He called her three times, at 5:10, 5:40 and 6:15.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel sitting with Papa on Monday?
qa.a: Vandana felt loving but trapped, as though the walls were pressing in.

qa.q: Which of Vandana's choices made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Asking Reena for a specific task, a daily video call and two weekends a month, shared the load instead of hoping for vague help.

qa.q: How might Reena feel after learning how often Papa called Vandana?
qa.a: Reena might feel guilty and surprised, which is why she agreed to regular calls and visits.

grounding: The story shows a young woman whose parent leans on her for company, feeling both love and being trapped, who asks her sibling for specific help and sets realistic limits.
